question: In the context of growing climate challenges, instability in international markets, rising production costs and increased competition from third-country agricultural imports, European farmers face increasing difficulty in maintaining competitiveness and sustainability.

At the same time, this sector needs to accelerate its green and digital transformation, meet environmental requirements, adapt to climate change and ensure food security for the European Union. The impact is particularly severe on small and medium-sized farms, which cannot easily access the financing, modern technologies, irrigation and innovations needed to increase their productivity and sustainability.

Against this backdrop, the European Commission needs to present a clear vision for the future development of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and measures to support European farmers post-2027. In this regard, I wish to ask the European Commission: 1.

What measures does the Commission plan to take to enhance the competitiveness of European agricultural producers against the rising number of imports from third countries not bound by the same environmental and production standards as EU Member States?

Does the Commission plan to establish additional financial mechanisms to support investments in modernisation, digitalisation, irrigation infrastructure and the adoption of innovative technologies in agriculture, particularly for small and medium-sized farms?

How does the European Commission assess the impact of climate change on food security in the European Union, and what additional measures does it intend to take to help farmers adapt to droughts, extreme weather events and water shortages in the coming years?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.8.2026) Imported food must comply with EU food safety import requirements, which are enforced through rigorous controls and audits that have recently been reinforced1. The Commission will pursue2, in line with international rules3, a stronger alignment of production standards applied to imported products, notably on pesticides and animal welfare.

The next multiannual financial framework proposals4 support agricultural innovation and competitiveness, notably via investments under the national and regional partnership (NRP) plans. The future Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) proposals5 – including for CAP implementing conditions and common market organisation – provide Member States with instruments to support agricultural investments.

Both streamline rules for smaller operations via compulsory simplified cost options. Within the NRP, the CAP can leverage synergies in knowledge, innovation and skills to enhance the sector’s competitiveness, sustainability and resilience, alongside vocational training, digitalisation, and other policy areas promoting digital skills and advanced farming practices.

In line with the Commission proposals, farming should also benefit from the European Competitiveness Fund and the Horizon Europe 2028-2034, with around EUR 40 billion available to foster research and innovation, competitiveness, sustainability, resilience, and fairness. The CAP proposal maintains robust decoupled income support, helping farmers adapt to changing conditions by stabilizing income.

It incentivizes risk management tools to share risks for bigger losses, resilient investments to reduce risk, and compulsory use of transition actions to cover costs of a more fundamental change of production system.
1 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/es/ip_25_2979. 2 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European economic and

social Committee and the Committee of the Regions A Vision for Agriculture and Food Shaping together an attractive farming and agri-food sector for future generations, COM/2025/75 final. 3 Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council - Application of EU health and environmental standards to imported agricultural and agri-food products, COM/2022/226 final.
